summary: Defines a YANG data model for managing network interfaces, including both configuration and state data such as status and counters. It is meant as a generic base that interface-type-specific models can extend. It was replaced by RFC 8343.

eli5.summary: Every network plug on a device needs a standard list of settings and meters. This document is the standard form for describing them so tools can read and change them. It was later replaced by a newer form.

questions: how to configure interfaces with netconf
subtitle: A standard way to describe and manage network interfaces in device configuration systems.

tldr.problem: Network devices need a standardized way to configure and monitor network interfaces. SNMP's IF-MIB worked but is limited by its design; a modern data model language is needed.
tldr.mechanism: YANG is a data modeling language for NETCONF. RFC 7223 defines the 'ietf-interfaces' YANG module with both configuration (writable) and state (read-only) sections for network interfaces. Type-specific models can extend it.
tldr.outcome: Provides a vendor-neutral, programmatic way to manage interfaces via NETCONF. The model was later superseded by RFC 8343 with improvements and extensions.

today: RFC 7223 was a Proposed Standard published in May 2014. It was replaced by RFC 8343, which provides an updated version with improved functionality and compatibility with YANG 1.1. The ietf-interfaces model remains widely used in network management systems.

sections.title: Introduction to YANG for Interfaces
sections.content:
RFC 7223 defines the ietf-interfaces YANG module, which provides a standardized way to manage network interfaces. YANG is a data modeling language for the NETCONF protocol, designed to replace or complement older management methods like SNMP.

Network interfaces are central to managing Internet protocols and devices. Rather than each vendor using proprietary methods, this RFC establishes a common data model for how interfaces are identified, configured, and monitored. The model includes both configuration data (settings an administrator controls) and state data (information about what the interface is actually doing, plus statistics).
sections.eli5: Every device has network plugs, and they all need the same basic information: what they are, whether they are on or off, and how much data moved through them. This defines a standard notebook for writing that down.

sections.title: Design Objectives
sections.content:
The YANG module design had several key goals. First, it needed to be simple enough that vendors with existing proprietary systems could map it to their own models. Second, new systems should be able to adopt it as-is without modifications.

Interface references needed to be straightforward, ideally using a single pointer by name. The model also needed to map clearly to SNMP's existing IF-MIB so that systems running both protocols could stay synchronized. Critically, the model had to support interface layering: both simple cases where one interface sits on top of another, and complex cases where multiple interfaces are aggregated together or multiplexed.

Pre-provisioning support was important—administrators should be able to configure an interface even if the hardware does not yet exist on the device. The model also needed to handle both physical interfaces (hardware plugs) and logical interfaces (virtual networks).
sections.eli5: The design needed to be simple so old systems could translate it, yet complete enough for new systems. It had to say clearly which plug sits on top of which, handle virtual plugs, and let you set up a plug before the hardware arrives.

sections.title: The Interface Data Hierarchy
sections.content:
The ietf-interfaces module has two main containers. The /interfaces subtree holds configuration: what administrators have explicitly set up. The /interfaces-state subtree is read-only and shows the live state of every interface on the device, plus statistics.

Each interface is identified by a unique name and has a mandatory type field indicating what kind of interface it is (Ethernet, loopback, virtual, and so forth). The type uses identities defined in the companion iana-if-type module, which aligns with SNMP's interface type registry.

Configuration data includes the name, description, type, whether the interface is enabled, and optionally which SNMP traps to send for link state changes. State data shows the administrative status (what was requested), operational status (what is actually happening), when the status last changed, the SNMP ifIndex number for compatibility, physical address if applicable, layer references (what sits on top and what sits below), speed, and detailed statistics counters.
sections.eli5: There are two lists: one for what you have configured, and one showing what is really happening now. Each lists the plug's name, type, whether it is on, and numbers for how much data passed through.

sections.title: Statistics and Counters
sections.content:
The state section includes a statistics container with detailed counters for monitoring interface health. Inbound counters track octets (bytes) and packets received, broken into unicast, broadcast, and multicast categories, plus discarded and errored packets, and packets with unknown protocols.

Outbound counters mirror these: octets and packets transmitted in unicast, broadcast, and multicast, plus discards and errors. The 64-bit counters accommodate high-speed modern interfaces. A discontinuity timestamp marks when the counters may have reset, helping administrators distinguish genuine traffic patterns from counter resets after hardware reboots.

Unlike the older IF-MIB which offered both 32-bit and 64-bit versions, this model provides only 64-bit counters, suitable for contemporary high-speed links.
sections.eli5: The counters measure what went in and out: how many pieces of data, grouped by type (broadcast vs. regular). A timestamp says when the numbers were last reset, so a sudden drop in numbers makes sense.

sections.title: Extension and Mapping
sections.content:
The ietf-interfaces module is intentionally generic and serves as a base for other modules. Vendors and standards bodies define type-specific modules that use YANG's augment operation to attach extra leaves and containers to the base model. For example, an Ethernet module would add duplex mode, speed negotiation, and MAC address settings specific to Ethernet interfaces.

These augmentations are conditional: they only apply when the interface type matches. An Ethernet augmentation would only be relevant when type = 'ethernetCsmacd'. Similarly, interface layering is defined not in the base model but in type-specific modules; a VLAN module would define how VLAN interfaces reference their underlying Ethernet interface.

The model maps cleanly to SNMP's IF-MIB when both are in use. Each entry in the state list typically maps to one ifEntry, and the if-index leaf carries the corresponding ifIndex value. The interface name maps to ifName, though subtle differences exist: ifAlias is a historical mapping for descriptions, and MTU is left to type-specific modules rather than being in the base.
sections.eli5: Other modules can build on this foundation, adding plug-type-specific features without changing the base. A VLAN module says how VLAN plugs connect to Ethernet ones. This keeps the base small and lets different vendors add what they need.

sections.title: Security and Access Control
sections.content:
The YANG module is accessed via NETCONF, which uses SSH as its mandatory-to-implement secure transport. NETCONF's access control model (RFC 6536) allows administrators to grant or deny specific users access to particular data and operations.

The writable portions of the module are sensitive. The /interfaces/interface list controls which interfaces are configured, and unauthorized modifications could cause the device to ignore traffic it should process. The enabled leaf controls whether an interface is administratively active; unauthorized changes could disable critical links. Access to these data nodes MUST be restricted to trusted administrators. Write operations without proper protection could degrade network availability and integrity.
sections.eli5: Only trusted people should be able to change interface settings. If someone turns off the wrong plug, the network stops working. SSH protects the connection, and access control decides who can change what.
